claims.text: Post-melt-spinning sub-Tg annealing improves both glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
Sub-Tg annealing relaxes internal stresses in the amorphous alloy.
Sub-Tg annealing promotes beneficial short-range ordering that impedes crystallization.
Rapid quenching by melt-spinning can produce an amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
The proposed treatment is a hold at approximately 0.8Tg for 60–120 seconds immediately after production.
An oxidation-preventing atmosphere is required for the intervention to be effective.
Remaining below Tg permits stress relaxation without initiating crystallization.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration can trigger devitrification.
The treatment reduces free volume.
Slight atomic rearrangements during annealing preserve the overall disordered structure.
Favorable short-range order increases the energy barrier for crystallization.
The amorphous phase is metastable and crystallizes when sufficient thermal energy overcomes an activation barrier.
Annealed samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than non-annealed controls.
DSC can identify the onset of exothermic crystallization in an amorphous high-entropy alloy.
The beneficial effect occurs only near 0.8Tg and within a 60–120 second treatment window.
Insufficient annealing will not adequately relieve internal stresses.
The optimal annealing temperature and duration vary with alloy composition.
Melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits diffuse diffraction features associated with short-range ordering in an amorphous structure.
Phosphorus influences the amorphization tendency of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
XRD and TEM can assess amorphous diffraction and short-range-order features, but the cited records do not establish them as measurements of annealing-induced internal-stress relaxation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the process a staged annealing treatment, whereas the intervention specifies only one isothermal hold and no stages.

The intervention is applied after an amorphous ribbon has already been formed, yet it is claimed to improve glass-forming ability, which concerns formation during processing; the experiment measures post-formation stability rather than glass-forming ability.
